(Sybex, 2020), book pages 251 to 288. It covers Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), the STP versions, Rapid PVST+, bridge ID changes, STP failures, PortFast, BPDU Guard and EtherChannel (LACP and PAgP, Layer 2 and Layer 3). Every difference from the book is tagged and listed in the Changes and Gaps Log.

After this chapter you should be able to:
Configure and verify Layer 2 and Layer 3 EtherChannel using LACP (objective 2.4).

Describe why Rapid PVST+ is needed and how it basically works (objective 2.5): root port, root bridge (primary and secondary), other port names, port states (forwarding and blocking), and the benefits of PortFast.

The STP examples in this chapter (Figures 9.10 and 9.12 and two new paper labs) were recomputed with a Python script that elects the root bridge, finds root ports by lowest path cost, and picks designated ports by path cost, then bridge ID, then port. The script agrees with the book on the final port roles but found a wrong reasoning step in the book (see Section 9.2.2 and the Gaps Log).

Routers stop loops at Layer 3 with the TTL field. Switches have no such field. If you connect switches in a ring, a broadcast frame can travel round and round forever.
STP exists to stop loops at Layer 2
by turning off redundant links, while keeping them ready as backups.
Without STP, redundant switch links cause three problems:
(the same source MAC is seen on different ports again and again). STP uses the spanning-tree algorithm (STA) to build a loop-free tree and blocks the links that are not in the tree.

Redundant links are good design (if one fails, another takes over). STP lets you have the redundancy without the loop. Everything in this chapter is about choosing which links to keep and how fast the switch recovers.

Figure 9.1 shows three switches (S1, S2, S3) joined in a triangle, which is a loop. Figure 9.2 shows the same network with STP: one of the three links is blocked, so the loop is gone. IEEE 802.1D is the default STP on Cisco IOS switches (really the Cisco PVST+ version of it).
The switch with the lowest (best) bridge ID. All decisions are made from its point of view. Every port on the root bridge is a designated (forwarding) port. The root bridge never has a root port.
Every other switch. Each one must have exactly one root port.
Bridge Protocol Data Unit. The STP message that switches send to each other. It carries the bridge ID. By default a BPDU is sent every 2 seconds (the hello time) out each active port.
8 bytes: bridge priority plus the switch base MAC address. Default priority is 32768. Lowest wins.
The cost of one link, based on its speed. Faster link, lower cost.
The sum of the port costs along the way to the root bridge.
The one port on a non-root switch with the lowest path cost to the root. Tie: lower upstream bridge ID, then lower upstream port number.
The port that has the best (lowest) path to the root on a segment. One per segment.
Everything left over. In 802.1D this is a blocked port.
Does not forward. Still listens to BPDUs, drops everything else, never sends frames.
Connected to a segment where another switch holds the designated port. It is a backup path to the root.

Alternate = another switch is the designated one (alternative path to the root). Backup = same switch, redundant link to the same segment (a backup of my own designated port). Backup ports are rare: they need a hub or shared segment.

This is why a new host sees an amber light for a long time and may fail to get a DHCP address: the port walks through listening and learning first. The book says this takes almost a minute.

Max age 20 s + listening 15 s + learning 15 s = 50 s (a script confirmed the sum). That is the worst case when a link failure is detected by a missing BPDU. To carry the VLAN number, PVST+ takes bits from the priority field. The priority becomes
(the VLAN ID). Only the top 4 bits are free to set, so priority comes in steps of 2^12 =

26 original questions with answers. Also do the book's own 10 review questions (pages 285 to 287) and check them in the Appendix (page 795). Read the Gaps Log first: book question 2 and its appendix answer contain an error.
A show output says Priority 28682 (priority 28672 sys-id-ext 10). Which VLAN is it and how was the priority probably set?
Does the root bridge have a root port?
C - The root bridge has none; every other switch has exactly one.
Which is a valid bridge priority?
B - Multiples of 4096 from 0 to 61440. 20480 = 5 x 4096.
A switch reaches the root over a 100 Mb/s link and then a 1 Gb/s link. What is the path cost (short method)?
Which two port roles replace the 802.1D blocking role in 802.1w?
Alternate and backup - Both are discarding ports.
How many port states does RSTP have, and what are they?
Three: discarding, learning, forwarding - Disabled, blocking and listening all map to discarding.
Break down the 50 second 802.1D worst case convergence time.
20 s max age + 15 s listening + 15 s learning - Sum verified by script.
What is the default STP hello time?
B - BPDUs go out every 2 seconds.
In PVST+, how many bits are priority and how many are the system ID extension?
4 bits priority, 12 bits system ID extension - That is why priority moves in steps of 4096.
Which command lists the VLANs for which this switch is root?
show spanning-tree summary - Look for the Root bridge for line.
What does protocol ieee mean in show spanning-tree output?
B - In rapid-pvst mode it says rstp.
State the main benefit of PortFast.
The port goes to forwarding immediately - Avoids the 30 to 50 s wait that can make DHCP fail.
A PortFast port with BPDU Guard receives a BPDU. What happens?
The port goes err-disabled - Recover with shutdown then no shutdown, or errdisable recovery.
Why should BPDU Guard not be put on a switch-to-switch uplink?
A real switch sends BPDUs, so the uplink would shut down - Use it on access ports only.
Which feature protects against a new switch winning the root election on a port?
B - Root guard blocks the port when a superior BPDU arrives.
Which feature protects against BPDUs suddenly stopping on a non-designated port?
C - Loop guard puts the port in loop-inconsistent instead of letting it forward.
Which mode combination will NOT form an LACP channel?
Which is the open standard: PAgP or LACP?
Which show etherchannel summary flags mean a healthy Layer 3 port channel with bundled members?
Po1(RU) and members (P) - R = Layer 3, U = in use, P = in the port channel.
Do two members of a channel need to have the same speed and duplex?
Yes - Also the same VLAN and trunk settings. Otherwise they can be suspended.
A bundle has 4 active links. One large file transfer between two hosts. How many links carry it?
One - The hash keeps a flow on a single link.
Why does a Layer 3 EtherChannel on a multilayer switch need no switchport?
To make the ports routed so they can carry an IP address - The IP goes on the port-channel interface.
Does an EtherChannel remove the need for STP?
No - STP still protects against misconfiguration and other loops.
Two switches both have priority 24576 in VLAN 1. MACs are 0000.AAAA.0001 and 0000.BBBB.0002. Which is the root?
Switches S1 (Rapid PVST+) and S2 (PVST+) are connected. What happens on that link?
It falls back to 802.1D-style behaviour on that port - Slow convergence on that link.
Is the port-channel number required to match on both ends of the link?
No, it is locally significant - The mode and settings must match, not the number.
